analogy.p: Think of a leaf as a **solar-powered factory**. The **transparent roof** (upper epidermis) lets sunlight in and keeps the weather out. The **production floor** at the top (palisade mesophyll) is packed with machines (chloroplasts) because that is where the sunlight lands. Underneath is a **storeroom with gaps between the shelves** (spongy mesophyll) where air can move around. **Delivery doors** (stomata) with **door staff** (guard cells) open and close to let materials in and out, and **pipes and lorries** (xylem and phloem) bring in water and take away the finished sugar. It breaks down because a factory is built and controlled by people, whereas a leaf's tissues form by **differentiation of cells from meristems**, and the leaf responds automatically to light, water and temperature.

bullets: **Plant tissues:** epidermal tissues, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem, phloem and meristem tissue.
**Meristem tissue** is found at the **growing tips of shoots and roots**.
**Plant organs:** **stems, roots and leaves**.
These organs make up **organ systems for transport of substances** (water, mineral ions and sugars) around the plant.
You must be able to **link structure to function** for each tissue and for the whole leaf.
Typical marks: 1 mark to name a tissue or label a diagram; 2 to 3 marks to explain how a leaf is adapted; 4 to 6 marks for an extended answer on leaf structure and function.

Link to other topics: cell differentiation and stem cells (meristems), photosynthesis (palisade cells, chloroplasts), transpiration and translocation (xylem, phloem), and gas exchange (stomata, air spaces).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA expects you to **describe the main tissues of a plant** and to **explain how they are organised into organs**. The tissues you must know are **epidermal tissues, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and meristem tissue found at the growing tips of shoots and roots**. The **organs** are the **stems, roots and leaves**, and together they form **organ systems for the transport of substances around the plant**. Questions test whether you can name a tissue from a description, link its structure to its function, and label a leaf cross-section.

bullets: **Waxy cuticle:** a thin waterproof layer on the **outer surface** of the upper epidermis. It **reduces water loss** by evaporation.

**Upper epidermis:** a single **transparent** layer of cells at the **top** of the leaf. It lets **light pass through** to the cells below and **protects** the leaf. In most leaves it has **few or no stomata**.

**Palisade mesophyll:** **tall, tightly packed cells** directly **beneath the upper epidermis**, with the **most chloroplasts**. They sit where the **light is strongest**, so most photosynthesis happens here.

**Spongy mesophyll:** **rounded, loosely packed cells** in the **lower middle** of the leaf with **air spaces** between them. The air spaces let **gases diffuse** through the leaf to and from the photosynthesising cells.

**Vein (vascular bundle):** runs **through the spongy mesophyll**. In a leaf cross-section **xylem is on the upper side and phloem on the lower side** of the vein. Xylem brings water in; phloem carries sugars away.
**Lower epidermis:** the layer at the **bottom** of the leaf. Most **stomata** are found here, where it is **cooler and shadier**, so **less water evaporates**.

**Stoma and guard cells:** a stoma is a **pore in the lower epidermis**, with a **pair of guard cells** on either side that open and close it. Do **not** confuse it with the **air spaces**, which are the gaps between spongy mesophyll cells.

**Path of carbon dioxide:** air outside → **open stoma** → **air spaces** in the spongy mesophyll → diffuses into the **palisade cells** (and the other mesophyll cells) → **chloroplasts**. **Oxygen** and **water vapour** diffuse out by the reverse route.

**Link to function:** the **thin** leaf gives a **short diffusion distance** and the **flat shape** a **large surface area**, so the layers are arranged to get **light in at the top** and **gases in at the bottom**.
core.h: Leaf cross-section: where every tissue is located (top to bottom)
core.p: Examiners often give a **diagram of a leaf cross-section** and ask you to **label** it or **say where a structure is found**, so you must picture the leaf as a stack of layers. Light arrives from above, so the layers are in the order light meets them: **waxy cuticle**, **upper epidermis**, **palisade mesophyll**, **spongy mesophyll** (with the **veins** running through it) and finally the **lower epidermis**, where the **stomata** are. Learn this order and you can place any structure and explain why it sits there. Study **Figure 1** while reading this section, then cover the labels and try to draw it from memory.

bullets: **Cell** (palisade cell) → **tissue** (palisade mesophyll) → **organ** (leaf) → **organ system** (transport system) → **organism** (whole plant).
A **tissue** contains cells of a **similar type** doing the same job; an **organ** contains **several different tissues**.
The leaf is an organ because it contains epidermis, mesophyll, xylem and phloem working together.
Specialised cells make each tissue efficient, which is why **differentiation** matters in plants.
Plants have **fewer organ systems** than animals, but transport is essential because the roots, stem and leaves are far apart.
Organisation allows **different jobs to happen in different places**: photosynthesis in leaves, absorption in roots, support and transport in stems.
Exam tip: use the exact definitions above, always saying tissues have **similar** cells and organs have **different** tissues.
core.h: Levels of organisation in a plant
core.p: Plants, like animals, are made of **cells that group into tissues, which group into organs, which group into organ systems**, which together make up the **organism**. A **cell** is the basic unit, for example a palisade cell. A **tissue** is a group of cells with a similar structure and function working together, for example palisade mesophyll. An **organ** is a group of different tissues that work together to carry out a particular job, for example a leaf. An **organ system** is a group of organs that work together to carry out a major function, such as the transport of substances around the plant.

bullets: Epidermal tissue **covers the surface** of the plant and **protects** the tissues underneath.
The **upper epidermis of a leaf is transparent** so that **light reaches the palisade cells**.
The **waxy cuticle** is a waterproof layer that **reduces water loss** by evaporation.
The **lower epidermis** contains the **guard cells** and **stomata**, through which gases diffuse.
Epidermal cells in leaves have **few or no chloroplasts**, so they do not block light or compete with the palisade layer.
Cells in the epidermis are **tightly packed**, forming a barrier against **microorganisms** entering.
In roots, some epidermal cells become **root hair cells** with a large surface area for absorption.
core.p: **Epidermal tissues** form the **outer covering** of the plant: the epidermis covers the **leaves, stems and roots**. In a leaf the epidermis has an **upper** and **lower** layer. The cells are flat and fit closely together, protecting the cells beneath. In the leaf the epidermis is covered by a **waxy cuticle**, a waterproof layer that **reduces water loss** by evaporation. The upper epidermis is **transparent** so light passes through to the photosynthetic cells below.

bullets: The palisade mesophyll is where **most photosynthesis** happens.
Cells are **tall and thin** and **arranged in a layer at the top of the leaf**, so they absorb **the maximum amount of light**.
Each cell contains **many chloroplasts** (chlorophyll absorbs light energy).
Chloroplasts can **move within the cell** to catch more light (an extra fact; not required).
The cells are **close to the upper epidermis**, which is transparent, so light reaches them easily.
Cells have **thin walls** so carbon dioxide can diffuse in quickly.
Word equation: **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen** (using light energy).
core.p: The **mesophyll** is the middle layer of the leaf where most photosynthesis takes place, and it has two parts. The **palisade mesophyll** is a layer of **tall, thin cells packed closely together** just below the upper epidermis. Palisade cells contain **lots of chloroplasts**, which contain **chlorophyll** to **absorb light** for photosynthesis. Their position at the **top** of the leaf means they receive the most light, and their column shape allows a lot of them to fit in a small area and gives a short path for light.

bullets: Cells are **rounded or irregular** and **loosely arranged**, leaving **air spaces**.
Air spaces give a **large internal surface area** for **diffusion of gases** between the cells and the air.
**Carbon dioxide** diffuses from the air spaces into the cells; **oxygen** produced in photosynthesis diffuses out into the air spaces.
Water **evaporates** from the surface of the cells into the air spaces; the water vapour then **diffuses out through the stomata** (transpiration).
The air spaces connect to the **stomata** in the lower epidermis.
Cells have a **thin, moist surface**, because gases dissolve before entering the cell.
The spongy layer is nearer the bottom of the leaf, so it receives **less light** than the palisade layer.
core.p: The **spongy mesophyll** is the layer of **loosely packed, irregularly shaped cells** below the palisade layer. Between the cells there are many **air spaces**. These air spaces give a **large surface area** for **gas exchange** and let **carbon dioxide diffuse** to the palisade cells and **oxygen and water vapour diffuse out**. The spongy mesophyll cells also contain some chloroplasts, but fewer than the palisade cells, so they photosynthesise less.

bullets: **Xylem:** water and mineral ions, **one direction (upwards)** from roots to leaves, in **hollow dead cells** with **lignin**.
**Phloem:** dissolved **sugars** (sucrose) from leaves to growing and storage regions, in **both directions**, in **living** cells.
The movement of water through the plant is the **transpiration stream** (covered in transpiration notes).
The movement of dissolved sugars is called **translocation**.
In a leaf, the veins **supply water for photosynthesis** and **carry away the sugars** made.
Together they form an **organ system for transport of substances** with the roots, stem and leaves.
Xylem and phloem are always **next to each other** in a vein, with xylem usually on the upper side in a leaf.
core.h: Xylem and phloem: the transport tissues
core.p: **Xylem** and **phloem** are the plant's **transport tissues**, found together in bundles called **veins** in the leaf and **vascular bundles** in the stem and root. **Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stem and leaves**. It is made of hollow tubes of dead cells strengthened with **lignin**, which also **supports the plant**. **Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant**, including the growing regions and storage organs. Phloem is made of living cells (sieve tube elements with companion cells), and substances can move in **both directions**.

bullets: Meristems are at the **tips of shoots** and **roots**, where the plant grows **longer**.
Meristem cells are **stem cells**: they divide by **mitosis** and can **differentiate into any type of plant cell**.
This ability lasts **throughout the life** of the plant, unlike most animal cells.
Because they are undifferentiated, they can be used in **tissue culture** to make plant **clones** quickly.
Meristem tissue in the **shoot tip** produces new leaves and stem; in the **root tip** it produces new root cells.
New cells made at the tips later **elongate** and **differentiate**, giving the mature tissues.
Link: stem cells (4.1.2) and cell differentiation.
core.p: **Meristem tissue** is found at the **growing tips of shoots and roots**. It contains **stem cells** that are **undifferentiated**, meaning they have not become specialised. The meristem cells **divide by mitosis** to make new cells, and these new cells can then **differentiate into the different types of plant cell** (such as xylem, phloem, palisade or root hair cells). In plants many cells keep the ability to differentiate throughout life, which is why plants can **keep growing** and why they can be **cloned** from cuttings.

bullets: **Upper epidermis:** transparent, covered by a **waxy cuticle**, protects and lets light in.
**Palisade mesophyll:** tall cells with **many chloroplasts**, where most **photosynthesis** occurs.
**Spongy mesophyll:** cells with **air spaces** for **gas exchange**.
**Xylem and phloem** in the veins: bring **water** and carry away **sugars**.
**Lower epidermis:** contains **stomata** with **guard cells**, mainly on the underside.
**Stomata:** pores that let **carbon dioxide in** and **oxygen and water vapour out**.
The **leaf's thin, flat shape** means a **large surface area** for light and a **short diffusion distance** for gases.
core.p: A **leaf** is an **organ** made of several tissues working together to carry out **photosynthesis**. From top to bottom it contains: the **upper epidermis**, the **palisade mesophyll**, the **spongy mesophyll** (with veins containing xylem and phloem running through) and the **lower epidermis** with **stomata** and **guard cells**. Each tissue has a specific function, and the way they are arranged makes the leaf **efficient at absorbing light and exchanging gases**. This is a classic 'structure and function' topic and is regularly tested with a labelled diagram.

bullets: **Broad, flat shape → large surface area** to **absorb more light**.
**Thin → short diffusion distance** for carbon dioxide to reach the cells.
**Palisade cells at the top with many chloroplasts → absorb the most light**.
**Air spaces in the spongy mesophyll → large surface area for gas exchange**.
**Stomata → let carbon dioxide in** and can **close to reduce water loss**.
**Veins (xylem and phloem) → supply water** (a reactant) and **remove glucose**.
**Transparent upper epidermis and thin waxy cuticle → light passes through** to the palisade cells.
core.h: How the leaf is adapted for photosynthesis
core.p: Examiners often ask you to **explain how a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis**. A full answer links each **structure** to its **function** and says **why** it helps. The leaf has a **large surface area** to absorb more light, it is **thin** so that **carbon dioxide has a short distance to diffuse** and light can reach all the cells, and it has **chloroplasts concentrated at the top** where the light is strongest. It has **air spaces** for gas diffusion, **stomata** that can open and close, and a **network of veins** that supplies water and removes sugars.

bullets: Stomata allow **carbon dioxide to enter** for photosynthesis and **oxygen and water vapour to leave**.
**Guard cells** control the size of the opening by changing shape.
Most stomata are on the **lower epidermis**, where it is **cooler and shadier**, so less water evaporates.
When guard cells are **turgid** the stoma is **open**; when **flaccid** the stoma is **closed**.
Closing the stomata **conserves water** but also **stops carbon dioxide entering**, slowing photosynthesis.
Guard cells have **chloroplasts**, unlike other epidermal cells.
Link: transpiration, osmosis and the effect of environmental conditions on water loss.
core.p: The **stomata** (singular: stoma) are tiny **pores**, mainly on the **underside** of the leaf, that allow **gases to diffuse in and out**. Each stoma is surrounded by a pair of **guard cells**, which can **change shape** to **open and close** the pore. When water is plentiful the guard cells become **turgid** and **open** the stoma. When water is short they become **flaccid** and **close** it, which **reduces water loss** by transpiration. The full detail of stomata and the transpiration rate is covered in the next spec points.

bullets: **Leaf:** photosynthesis and gas exchange; contains epidermis, mesophyll, xylem and phloem.
**Stem:** supports the plant and **transports** substances in **xylem and phloem**; holds leaves in a good position for **light**.
**Roots:** **anchor** the plant and **absorb water and mineral ions** from the soil.
**Root hair cells** (epidermal cells in the root) have a **large surface area** for absorption.
**Meristem tissue** at the **tips** of the shoots and roots produces new cells for growth.
Organs are connected by xylem and phloem, so **water travels up** and **sugars travel to where they are needed**.
If any organ is damaged the whole plant is affected, because **organs depend on each other**.
core.h: Plant organs: stems, roots and leaves
core.p: The three main **plant organs** are the **stem**, the **roots** and the **leaves**. Each is made of several tissues. The **leaf** carries out photosynthesis. The **stem** **supports** the plant, holds the leaves up to the light and contains the **xylem and phloem** that carry substances between the roots and leaves. The **roots** **anchor** the plant in the soil and **absorb water and mineral ions** through root hair cells. Together these organs form the **organ system** for transport of substances around the plant.

bullets: **Xylem** carries **water and mineral ions up** from roots to leaves.
**Phloem** carries **dissolved sugars** from leaves to all parts of the plant.
Roots **cannot photosynthesise**, because they are underground, so they **need sugars delivered** by the phloem.
Plants do not have a heart; movement of water is driven mainly by **evaporation from the leaves (transpiration)**.
Without transport, the **inner cells** would not receive what they need by diffusion alone, because plants are large with a small surface area to volume ratio.
The **organ system** concept: **organs** (root, stem, leaf) + **tissues** (xylem, phloem) working together.
Link: surface area to volume ratio (4.1.3) and why large organisms need transport systems.
core.h: Plants as organ systems and transport of substances
core.p: Plants need to move materials between organs because **different organs do different jobs and are far apart**. **Water and mineral ions** enter at the **roots** and must reach the **leaves**, where water is used in photosynthesis. **Sugars made in the leaves** must reach the **roots**, **growing tips** and storage organs, which cannot photosynthesise. The **organ system for transport** (roots, stem and leaves linked by xylem and phloem) carries out this movement. The details of the **transpiration stream** and **translocation** are covered in the next spec points.

bullets: **Name the tissue** from its description: transparent covering = upper epidermis; tall cells with lots of chloroplasts = palisade; air spaces = spongy mesophyll.
**Say what it does and why it helps**: feature → function → benefit.
**Do not mix up** xylem (water, mineral ions, dead, lignin) and phloem (sugars, living, both directions).
Do not say 'roots take in food': roots take in **water and mineral ions** (plants make their own food by photosynthesis).
Use **'diffusion'** for the movement of gases through the stomata and air spaces.
Refer to **chloroplasts** and **chlorophyll** when explaining light absorption.
For a 6-mark answer include structure, function, adaptation, and a linked idea such as water loss or gas exchange.
core.h: Exam skills: labelling and linking structure to function
core.p: A good answer always links **a named tissue** to **its function** and to **the feature that allows that function**. For example: 'The palisade mesophyll has many chloroplasts, so it absorbs a lot of light for photosynthesis.' When asked about a leaf, move **from top to bottom** through the layers in order, so that you do not leave anything out. When labelling, use the **exact names** from the specification and make sure label lines touch the correct layer. Use **comparative** words and give **reasons** (because, so that, which allows).

exam: **Name a tissue from a description (1 mark):** transparent covering = upper epidermis; lots of chloroplasts = palisade mesophyll; air spaces = spongy mesophyll; hollow dead tubes with lignin = xylem.

**Labelling a leaf cross-section:** work **top to bottom** - cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade (tall cells, most chloroplasts), spongy (air spaces, veins), lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells. Give the **location** (for example 'lower epidermis') as well as the name when asked 'where'. Xylem is on the **upper** side of a vein and phloem on the **lower** side.
**State the function (1 mark):** palisade = photosynthesis; spongy = gas exchange; xylem = water and mineral ions; phloem = dissolved sugars; meristem = growth by cell division/differentiation.
**Define tissue, organ and organ system (1 to 2 marks each):** tissue = group of similar cells; organ = group of different tissues; organ system = group of organs working together.
**Label a leaf cross-section (up to 4 marks):** upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, lower epidermis, stoma, guard cell, xylem, phloem. Make sure lines touch the correct layer.

**Explain how the leaf is adapted for photosynthesis (3 to 4 marks):** large flat surface area (absorbs light), thin (short diffusion distance), many chloroplasts in palisade cells at the top, air spaces and stomata for CO2, veins to supply water.
**Explain why palisade cells are at the top (2 marks):** that is where most light falls (1) so more light is absorbed for photosynthesis (1).
**Meristem questions (2 to 3 marks):** at the tips of shoots and roots, cells divide by mitosis, can differentiate into any type of plant cell, allow growth throughout life.
**Link xylem and phloem to the organ system (2 to 3 marks):** transport of water, mineral ions and sugars between roots, stem and leaves.
**Why do plants need transport systems? (2 marks):** large with a small surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion alone is too slow to supply inner cells.
**Command words:** State = one fact; Describe = say what; Explain = give a reason (because); Suggest = apply knowledge to a new context.
**6-mark plan:** list the layers from top to bottom, give each function and adaptation, then link to gas exchange and water loss.

mistakes.r: Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries dissolved sugars.
mistakes.w: Xylem carries sugars and phloem carries water.

mistakes.r: Roots absorb water and mineral ions; plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis.
mistakes.w: Roots take in food from the soil.

mistakes.r: Palisade mesophyll is near the top, just below the upper epidermis, to absorb the most light.
mistakes.w: Palisade cells are at the bottom of the leaf.

mistakes.r: Most photosynthesis happens in the palisade mesophyll; the spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gas exchange.
mistakes.w: Spongy mesophyll is where most photosynthesis happens.

mistakes.r: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is made of different tissues.
mistakes.w: A tissue is a group of different cells working together.

mistakes.r: Most stomata (with guard cells) are in the lower epidermis, which reduces water loss.
mistakes.w: The upper epidermis is where the stomata are.

mistakes.r: Xylem cells are dead and hollow with lignin; phloem is living tissue.
mistakes.w: Phloem cells are dead and hollow.

mistakes.r: Meristem tissue is found only at the growing tips of shoots and roots.
mistakes.w: Meristem is found all over the plant.

mistakes.r: The leaf is thin to give a short diffusion distance for gases and let light reach the cells.
mistakes.w: The leaf is thick so it can absorb more light.

mistakes.r: The air spaces are the gaps between spongy mesophyll cells. A stoma is a pore in the epidermis (mostly the lower epidermis) with a pair of guard cells that open and close it.
mistakes.w: The stoma is the hole or gap inside the leaf between the cells.

summary: AQA 4.2.3: you must know the plant tissues (epidermal tissues, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and meristem tissue at the growing tips of shoots and roots), that stems, roots and leaves are plant organs, and that these organs form organ systems for transporting substances around the plant. It matters because it applies the cells, tissues, organs and organ systems idea to plants and sets up transpiration, translocation, photosynthesis and gas exchange.

terms.d: A group of cells with a similar structure and function.
A group of different tissues that work together to perform a certain function.
A group of organs that work together to perform a certain function, for example the transport system of a plant.
Tissue that covers the surface of the plant; in a leaf the upper epidermis is transparent and the lower epidermis contains stomata.
A waterproof layer on the surface of the leaf epidermis that reduces water loss by evaporation.
Tissue made of tall, tightly packed cells containing many chloroplasts, where most photosynthesis takes place.
Tissue with loosely packed cells and air spaces that gives a large surface area for gas exchange.
Tissue made of hollow dead cells strengthened with lignin that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves.
Living tissue that transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
Tissue found at the growing tips of shoots and roots containing stem cells that can differentiate into any type of plant cell.
A pore, mainly on the underside of the leaf, through which gases diffuse in and out.
One of a pair of cells surrounding a stoma that changes shape to open and close it.
A sub-cellular structure containing chlorophyll; the site of photosynthesis.
A green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
A strong, waterproof substance in xylem walls that supports the plant.
The loss of water vapour from the leaves, mainly through the stomata, which draws water up the plant.
The transport of dissolved sugars in the phloem from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
A bundle of xylem and phloem that carries substances through the leaf, stem and root.

worked.ans: The leaf is broad and flat, giving a large surface area to absorb light, and thin, so carbon dioxide has a short diffusion distance. The palisade mesophyll at the top contains many chloroplasts, so the most light is absorbed there. The spongy mesophyll has air spaces and the lower epidermis has stomata, so carbon dioxide can diffuse in quickly, and xylem in the veins supplies water.
worked.q: Describe how the structure of a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. (4 marks)
steps: Large flat surface area so more light is absorbed.
Thin so carbon dioxide has a short distance to diffuse and light reaches all cells.
Palisade cells at the top contain many chloroplasts, so the maximum amount of light is absorbed.
Air spaces in the spongy mesophyll and stomata allow carbon dioxide to diffuse in; xylem brings water.

worked.ans: Xylem carries water and mineral ions up from the roots to the leaves, whereas phloem carries dissolved sugars made in the leaves to other parts of the plant. Plants need both because leaves need water for photosynthesis and the roots and growing tips cannot photosynthesise so must be supplied with sugars.
worked.q: A student states that the xylem and phloem carry the same substances. Correct this and explain why plants need both. (3 marks)
steps: Xylem carries water and mineral ions from roots to leaves.
Phloem carries dissolved sugars from leaves to the rest of the plant.
Both are needed because roots cannot photosynthesise (need sugars) and leaves need water and minerals.

worked.ans: Meristem tissue, found at the growing tips of the shoots and roots, contains stem cells that divide by mitosis. The new cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell, so the plant can keep growing throughout its life.
worked.q: Explain the role of meristem tissue in a plant. (3 marks)
steps: Meristem tissue is at the tips of the shoots and roots.
Its cells divide by mitosis, producing new cells.
These cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell, allowing the plant to keep growing.
